Meson. Mesons are hadrons composed of a quark-antiquark pair bound by gluon exchange. They carry integer spin and integer charge, obey Bose-Einstein statistics, and decay via the weak force. The pion and kaon are the lightest and most common mesons; together with baryons, they comprise the hadron family.

A meson consists of one quark and one antiquark. Mesons carry baryon number zero, meaning they have no barrier to decay based on baryon number conservation. Because they are composed of two fermions forming an integer-spin composite, they obey Bose-Einstein statistics. Mesons carry integer spin—zero, one, two—making them bosonic despite being made of fermions. The pion is the lightest meson and historically explained the range of the nuclear force. The kaon contains a strange quark and reveals flavor physics through its decays. The rho is an example of a vector meson with spin one. Most mesons decay within picoseconds via the weak force through flavor-changing processes. Meson pairs naturally combine opposite electric charges, one quark with one antiquark. Pseudoscalar and vector mesons dominate low-energy hadron phenomenology.

Mesons were the first composite particles predicted and observed, historically motivating the quark model itself. The pion, discovered in cosmic rays, explained the range of the nuclear force through Yukawa's meson exchange theory. Meson oscillations—kaon mixing and B meson oscillations—provide unique windows into CP violation and rare decays, essential for understanding matter-antimatter asymmetry in the universe.
